sets.title: Set 1: Original Exam Questions
sets.description: The original MCQs from the April 2024 class First Block Supplementary Exam paper (PHM 102: Pharmacology, Section A, Q1 to Q30).

questions.text: Common side effects of atrovent include:
questions.explanation: Dry mouth, blurred vision (B) is correct because Atrovent (ipratropium bromide) is an anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) bronchodilator. By blocking acetylcholine receptors it reduces secretions and causes the typical anticholinergic effects: dry mouth, blurred vision (especially if the spray gets into the eyes, and it can raise eye pressure in angle-closure glaucoma), urinary retention, constipation, palpitations or tachycardia, cough and headache. The patient is advised to rinse the mouth and sip water after use and to keep the spray away from the eyes. Salivation, diarrhea (A) are the opposite of anticholinergic effects. Bradycardia, headache (C) is incorrect because the pulse tends to speed up (tachycardia). Nausea, weight loss (D) are not typical.

questions.text: An example of a mucolytic drug is:
questions.explanation: Acetylcysteine (C) is correct because it is a mucolytic that breaks the disulphide bonds in the mucus proteins, making thick, sticky bronchial secretions thinner and easier to cough up. It is used in chronic bronchitis, COPD, cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis (and, by IV, as the antidote for paracetamol overdose). Other mucolytics are carbocisteine, bromhexine and ambroxol. Patients should drink plenty of fluids and expect more sputum at first. Benilyn (A) (Benylin) is a brand name for cough syrups, and Ascoril (B) is a brand of combination cough syrup (it contains bromhexine and guaifenesin with a bronchodilator), so they are product names and not a single mucolytic drug. Loratadine (D) is a second-generation antihistamine.

questions.text: A side effect of tetracycline is:
questions.explanation: Gastric irritation (B) is correct because tetracyclines commonly cause nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, diarrhoea and oesophageal irritation, which is why doses should be taken with a full glass of water, sitting upright, and not just before lying down. Tetracyclines also cause photosensitivity, staining of developing teeth and bone effects in children under 8 years (and in pregnancy), and overgrowth of Candida or other organisms (superinfection). Skin rash (A) can occur as a photosensitivity reaction and in hypersensitivity, but gastrointestinal upset is the most common effect. Palpitation (C) is not a feature. Gum bleeding (D) is not a typical effect, and tetracycline is not associated with bleeding.

questions.text: An antitussive with no sedative effect is:
questions.explanation: Dextromethorphan (C) is correct because it is a non-narcotic cough suppressant that raises the threshold of the cough centre in the medulla, and at normal doses it has no significant sedative, analgesic or respiratory depressant effect, and little risk of dependence. It should not be combined with MAO inhibitors or SSRIs (serotonin syndrome). Pholcodine (A) is an opioid-like cough suppressant that can cause mild drowsiness and constipation. Methadone (B) is a strong opioid analgesic that causes sedation and respiratory depression. Codeine (D) is an opioid that causes sedation, constipation and respiratory depression.

questions.text: Diazepam is used as a preanaethetic medication to:
questions.explanation: Relieve anxiety (A) is correct because diazepam is a benzodiazepine that enhances the effect of GABA, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain. Before surgery it relieves the patient's anxiety, produces calmness and sedation, and causes amnesia for the events around the operation. It also reduces the amount of anaesthetic needed. The nurse monitors for respiratory depression and excessive sedation, and flumazenil is the reversal agent. Dry up secretions (B) is the role of anticholinergics such as atropine and hyoscine. Increase alertness (C) is the opposite of the effect. Reduce pain (D) is the role of opioid analgesics, since diazepam has no pain-relieving effect.

questions.text: An example of antihistamine that does not cause sedation is:
questions.explanation: Loratadine (A) is correct because it is a second-generation H1 antihistamine, which does not cross the blood-brain barrier much, so it causes little or no drowsiness, and it is taken once daily. Chlorpheniramine (B), cyclizine (C) and promethazine (D) are first-generation antihistamines that enter the brain and cause sedation and anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention). Cyclizine and promethazine are also used as antiemetics, and their drowsiness is part of the reason they work for motion sickness and vomiting.

questions.text: The antibiotic that inhibit protein synthesis by acting on 50S subunit is:
questions.explanation: Erythromycin (D) is correct because it is a macrolide that binds the 50S subunit of the bacterial ribosome and blocks translocation of the growing peptide chain, so protein synthesis stops (bacteriostatic, sometimes bactericidal). Other 50S inhibitors include azithromycin, clarithromycin, clindamycin and chloramphenicol. Amoxicillin (A) and ceftriaxone (C) are beta-lactams that inhibit cell wall synthesis. Tetracycline (B) acts on the 30S subunit, where it blocks the attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA. Erythromycin often causes gastrointestinal upset (nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps) and can prolong the QT interval, and it inhibits liver enzymes, which raises the level of many other drugs.

questions.text: A true statement regarding the Benzyl penicillin is:

options.A: It is a narrow spectrum antibiotic
options.B: It is a broad spectrum antibiotic
options.C: Given alone in treatment of pneumonia
options.D: Cannot be hydrolyzed by beta lactamases

questions.explanation: It is a narrow spectrum antibiotic (A) is correct because benzyl penicillin (penicillin G) is mainly active against gram-positive bacteria (streptococci, pneumococci, many Neisseria and anaerobes) and a few others such as Treponema pallidum, but it has little activity against most gram-negative bacilli. It is a broad spectrum antibiotic (B) is incorrect, because broad-spectrum penicillins are the aminopenicillins (ampicillin, amoxicillin). Given alone in treatment of pneumonia (C) is not the best answer: although benzyl penicillin alone is used for some pneumococcal and non-severe pneumonia cases, it is usually combined with gentamicin in severe pneumonia in Kenyan guidelines, and it does not cover atypical organisms, so the statement is not generally true. Cannot be hydrolyzed by beta lactamases (D) is incorrect because benzyl penicillin is easily destroyed by beta-lactamases (penicillinases) from organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, which is why cloxacillin or flucloxacillin is needed for those. It is destroyed by stomach acid, so it is given by injection (IV or IM).

questions.text: First generation Cephalosporins:

options.A: Have strong activity against gram-negative bacteria
options.C: Are strongly active against gram positive bacteria

questions.explanation: Are strongly active against gram positive bacteria (C) is correct because first-generation cephalosporins (cefazolin, cephalexin, cefadroxil) are most active against gram-positive cocci (methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci), and have only modest activity against a few gram-negative organisms (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus). They are used for skin and soft tissue infections, uncomplicated UTI and surgical prophylaxis (cefazolin). Have strong activity against gram-negative bacteria (A) is incorrect because gram-negative activity increases with the later generations. Are resistant to beta lactamases (B) is incorrect because they are stable against staphylococcal penicillinase but are destroyed by many gram-negative beta-lactamases, and resistance to beta-lactamases improves from the second generation on. Have extended spectrum against klebsiella (D) is incorrect because extended gram-negative coverage belongs to the third generation.

questions.text: When administering ciprofloxacin for a patient with UTI, the nurse should encourage the patient to:

options.B: Eat immediately after taking the medication
options.C: Avoid voiding to allow the drug to act
options.D: Take food rich in vitamin A

questions.explanation: Take plenty of water (A) is correct because ciprofloxacin is excreted mostly by the kidneys, and good hydration helps to flush the urinary tract and clear the infection, keeps the urine dilute, and reduces the risk of crystalluria (crystals forming in concentrated, alkaline urine). Patients should also avoid taking it together with dairy products, antacids, iron, calcium or zinc (they chelate the drug and reduce absorption, so ciprofloxacin is taken 2 hours before or 6 hours after them), and be told to stop and report tendon pain (tendinitis and tendon rupture), photosensitivity and dizziness. Eat immediately after taking the medication (B) is not needed, and dairy-containing meals reduce absorption. Avoid voiding to allow the drug to act (C) is incorrect because the patient should void regularly to flush bacteria out, and holding urine encourages bacterial growth. Take food rich in vitamin A (D) has no relevance.

questions.text: The antifungal Nystatin is indicated for children with:
questions.explanation: Oral thrush (D) is correct because nystatin is a polyene antifungal that binds ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane and is not absorbed from the gut or mucous membranes, so it acts locally on Candida in the mouth and gut. For infants and children, the suspension is dropped into the mouth after feeds and swabbed on the lesions, kept in contact with the mouth as long as possible, and continued for 2 days after the lesions have cleared. Cryptococcal meningitis (A) needs amphotericin B and fluconazole. Histoplasmosis (B) needs itraconazole or amphotericin B. Tinea capitis (C) is a scalp dermatophyte infection that needs oral griseofulvin or terbinafine, and nystatin is not active against dermatophytes.

questions.text: A non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor is:
questions.explanation: Nevirapine (A) is correct because it is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI), which binds directly to a site on HIV reverse transcriptase and changes the shape of the enzyme so that it cannot make DNA from viral RNA. It can cause rash (sometimes severe, Stevens-Johnson syndrome) and hepatotoxicity, so it is started with a 14-day lead-in dose. Enfuvirtide (B) is a fusion inhibitor given by subcutaneous injection that stops HIV from entering cells. Stavudine (C) and didanosine (D) are nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs); they cause peripheral neuropathy, lipoatrophy, lactic acidosis and pancreatitis (didanosine), and are now rarely used.

questions.text: A side effect of intravenous quinine administration is:
questions.explanation: Hypoglycaemia (B) is correct because quinine stimulates the beta cells of the pancreas to release insulin, and severe malaria itself also reduces blood glucose, so patients (especially children and pregnant women) are at high risk of low blood sugar. IV quinine is therefore diluted in 5% dextrose and given as a slow infusion over about 4 hours, with regular blood glucose checks (and treatment of low glucose with IV dextrose). Rapid injection can also cause hypotension and arrhythmias. Cinchonism (tinnitus, headache, nausea, blurred vision) occurs with higher doses. Palpitation (A) can occur with arrhythmias but is not the key side effect. Dark urine (C) is more typical of haemolysis (blackwater fever) or primaquine. Headache (D) is a general effect of cinchonism, not the specific one for the IV route.

questions.text: Monoclonal antibodies:
questions.explanation: Destroy cancerous cells (C) is the best answer because monoclonal antibodies are laboratory-made antibodies, each designed to recognise one specific antigen. In cancer treatment they attach to proteins on the surface of cancer cells (for example rituximab to CD20 on B-cell lymphoma, trastuzumab to HER2 in breast cancer) and either mark the cell for destruction by the immune system, block growth signals, or carry a toxin or radioactive particle to the cell, so they are targeted therapy with fewer effects on normal cells than ordinary chemotherapy. Side effects include infusion reactions (fever, chills, hypotension), so the nurse monitors closely during the infusion and may give premedication. Fight infection (A) is a use for a few monoclonals (for example palivizumab for RSV), but it is not their main use. Increase number of lymphocytes (B) is not their action. Antagonize antineoplastics (D) is the opposite; they work alongside chemotherapy.

questions.text: The adverse effect of antineoplastic agents includes:
questions.explanation: Alopecia, anaemia (A) is correct because antineoplastic (cytotoxic) drugs damage rapidly dividing cells, which include cancer cells but also normal hair follicle cells (causing alopecia, which is usually reversible) and bone marrow cells (causing myelosuppression, with anaemia, leucopenia and thrombocytopenia, so infection and bleeding risks). Other common effects are nausea and vomiting, mucositis (mouth sores), diarrhoea, fatigue, and in some cases cardiotoxicity, nephrotoxicity or neuropathy, and some cause infertility and are teratogenic. The nurse monitors blood counts, gives antiemetics, supports oral hygiene and protects against infection. Hypermelaninomia, Scotoma (B) are not typical. High blood pressure, hepatotoxicity (C) are not the typical pair, since low blood counts are the key effect. Gastric irritation, weight loss (D) are less specific and incomplete, as they omit the bone marrow effects.

questions.text: Contra indication of Vitamin D supplements include:
questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia (B) is correct because vitamin D increases calcium absorption from the gut and calcium release from bone, so it can worsen a high blood calcium level and cause calcium deposits in the kidneys and soft tissues, kidney stones and kidney damage. Signs of toxicity are nausea, vomiting, constipation, thirst, polyuria, weakness and confusion. It is also contraindicated in vitamin D toxicity (hypervitaminosis D) and with care in sarcoidosis and kidney stones. Hyperglycemia (A) and hypomagnesemia (C) are not contraindications. Hypovitaminosis (D) is an indication (vitamin D deficiency, rickets, osteomalacia), since the supplements treat it.

questions.text: A patient who is on calcium supplements should be informed to:

options.A: Take them in combination with iron supplements
options.B: Always monitor for signs of hypertension
options.C: Take with a full glass of water

questions.explanation: Take with a full glass of water (C) is correct because calcium supplements (especially calcium carbonate) are taken with a full glass of water (and with food, since calcium carbonate needs stomach acid for absorption) to help the tablet dissolve, aid absorption and reduce constipation and the risk of kidney stones. Doses are split (not more than about 500 mg at a time). Take them in combination with iron supplements (A) is incorrect because calcium reduces iron absorption, so they should be taken about 2 hours apart. Always monitor for signs of hypertension (B) is not an effect, but patients should watch for signs of high calcium (nausea, thirst, polyuria, confusion, constipation). Monitor for diarrhea (D) is incorrect because calcium commonly causes constipation and bloating, and not diarrhoea.

questions.text: Thiamine supplements are used in the treatment of:
questions.explanation: Beriberi (B) is correct because thiamine (vitamin B1) is a coenzyme needed for carbohydrate metabolism, and its deficiency causes beriberi: wet beriberi affects the heart (heart failure, oedema), and dry beriberi affects the nerves (peripheral neuropathy, muscle wasting). Thiamine is also given to prevent and treat Wernicke's encephalopathy in alcohol dependence, and in malnutrition. Pellagra (A) is caused by niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia). Scurvy (C) is caused by vitamin C deficiency. Marasmus (D) is severe protein-energy malnutrition and is treated with nutritional rehabilitation, not thiamine alone.

questions.text: Nitrofurantoin:

options.D: It is not recommended for Upper UTIs

questions.explanation: It is not recommended for Upper UTIs (D) is the best answer. Nitrofurantoin is rapidly absorbed and excreted by the kidneys, so it reaches high concentrations in the urine but very low concentrations in the blood and kidney tissue. It is therefore effective for cystitis (lower UTI) but not for pyelonephritis or any infection above the bladder, and it is ineffective in significant renal impairment. Common effects are nausea, brown urine, peripheral neuropathy and, with long-term use, lung and liver reactions; it is avoided in G6PD deficiency and near term in pregnancy. Leads to tendinitis (A) is incorrect, since tendon rupture is an effect of fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin. Predispose patients to crystalluria (C) is incorrect, since crystalluria is typical of sulfonamides such as co-trimoxazole. Works best in acidic environment (B) is also a true pharmacological statement, because nitrofurantoin is more active in acidic urine, but the defining clinical limitation is that it is not used for upper urinary tract infections. Note: because both B and D are true, D is chosen as the more clinically important statement.

questions.text: Captopril:
questions.explanation: Decrease peripheral vascular resistance (C) is correct because captopril is an ACE inhibitor. It blocks the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, so there is less vasoconstriction, and the arterioles and veins relax, which lowers peripheral vascular resistance (afterload) and blood pressure; less aldosterone also means that less sodium and water are retained (reducing preload). It is used in hypertension, heart failure and after myocardial infarction. Side effects include dry cough, first-dose hypotension, hyperkalaemia, taste disturbance, rash and angioedema, and it is contraindicated in pregnancy. Increase cardiac workload (A) is incorrect because the drug reduces the workload of the heart. Causes ventricular remodeling (B) is incorrect because ACE inhibitors prevent and reverse harmful remodeling of the heart after infarction and in heart failure. Is associated with rebound tachycardia (D) is incorrect because reflex tachycardia occurs with direct vasodilators such as hydralazine and nifedipine, but ACE inhibitors do not trigger it.

questions.text: The group of antihypertensive drugs which reduces the metabolism of bradykinin is:
questions.explanation: Angiotensin Converting Enzyme Inhibitors (C) is correct because ACE is also the enzyme (kininase II) that breaks down bradykinin, a vasodilator peptide. When ACE inhibitors such as captopril, enalapril and lisinopril block the enzyme, bradykinin accumulates, which adds to their blood pressure lowering effect, but also causes the typical side effects of persistent dry cough and angioedema (swelling of the lips, tongue and throat, which is an emergency). If cough is troublesome, the patient is switched to an angiotensin II receptor blocker such as losartan. Calcium channel blockers (A) block calcium entry into cells. Beta blockers (B) block beta receptors. Diuretics (D) increase excretion of sodium and water, and none of them affects bradykinin breakdown.

questions.text: An example of alpha II-adrenergic receptor blocker is:
questions.explanation: Aldomet (B) is the best answer. Aldomet is the brand name of methyldopa, a centrally acting antihypertensive that is converted to alpha-methylnorepinephrine, which stimulates alpha-2 adrenergic receptors in the brainstem, reducing sympathetic outflow, heart rate and peripheral resistance, so blood pressure falls. Strictly speaking, methyldopa acts as an alpha-2 agonist (clonidine is the other example), and the paper's word 'blocker' refers to the alpha-2 receptor group of antihypertensives. Methyldopa is commonly used for hypertension in pregnancy, and its side effects are sedation, dry mouth, postural hypotension, depression, hepatotoxicity and a positive Coombs test with haemolytic anaemia. Lisinopril (A) and enalapril (C) are ACE inhibitors. Nifedipine (D) is a calcium channel blocker.

questions.text: Long term use of hydralazine leads to:
questions.explanation: Systemic Lupus erythematous (C) is correct because long-term, high-dose hydralazine (usually more than 200 mg a day), especially in slow acetylators and women, can cause a drug-induced lupus-like syndrome with joint pain, fever, rash, pleurisy and positive antinuclear antibodies. It usually resolves when the drug is stopped. Hydralazine is a direct arteriolar vasodilator used in severe hypertension and pre-eclampsia, and its common effects are headache, palpitations and reflex tachycardia, and fluid retention, so it is combined with a beta blocker and a diuretic. Hypotension (A) is the immediate expected effect rather than a long-term complication. Resistance (B) is not the characteristic long-term effect. Hyperkalemia (D) is a feature of ACE inhibitors and potassium-sparing diuretics.

questions.text: The drug that stimulates alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptors to manage cardiogenic and septic shock is:
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine (A) is correct because it stimulates alpha-1 receptors (strong vasoconstriction, which raises blood pressure) and beta-1 receptors (increases the force of contraction of the heart). It is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock after fluids, and is used in cardiogenic shock when blood pressure is low. It is given by IV infusion through a central line where possible, and the nurse monitors blood pressure continuously and checks the site often, because extravasation causes severe tissue necrosis (phentolamine is the antidote). Manitol (B), mannitol, is an osmotic diuretic. Nitrite (C) (nitrates) are vasodilators used for angina and heart failure, and they would lower blood pressure. Ramipril (D) is an ACE inhibitor, which lowers blood pressure and is not used in shock.

questions.text: A loop diuretic alternative to patients allergic to furosemide is:
questions.explanation: Ethacrynic acid (D) is correct because furosemide, bumetanide and torsemide are chemically related to sulfonamides, so they may cause cross-reaction in a patient with sulfonamide allergy. Ethacrynic acid is a loop diuretic that is not a sulfonamide (it is a phenoxyacetic acid derivative), so it can be used as an alternative loop diuretic in these patients, although it has a higher risk of ototoxicity (deafness and tinnitus) and gastrointestinal upset. Isosorbide (A) is a nitrate vasodilator and not a diuretic. Torsenide (B), torsemide, and bumetanide (C) are both loop diuretics, but they are sulfonamide derivatives and so are not safe alternatives in true sulfonamide allergy (although cross-reactivity is low).

questions.text: Calcium channel blockers:

options.A: Decrease the contractility of the myocardium

questions.explanation: Improve myocardial perfusion (C) is the best answer because all calcium channel blockers block the entry of calcium into smooth muscle cells of the coronary and peripheral arteries, causing vasodilation: the coronary arteries dilate (and coronary spasm is prevented), which improves blood flow and oxygen supply to the heart muscle, and the peripheral arterioles dilate, which lowers afterload and oxygen demand. This is why they are used in angina and hypertension. Increase peripheral resistance (B) is incorrect because they lower it. Increase venous returns (D) is incorrect because they mainly dilate arteries and have little effect on veins, unlike nitrates. Decrease the contractility of the myocardium (A) is true mainly for the non-dihydropyridines (verapamil and diltiazem), which also slow the heart, whereas dihydropyridines such as nifedipine and amlodipine have little effect on contractility. Note: both A and C describe real effects, but C applies to the whole class.

questions.text: The anti-coagulant of choice in pregnancy is:
questions.explanation: Heparin (A) is correct because it is a large, highly charged molecule that does not cross the placenta, so it does not affect the fetus. Low molecular weight heparin (for example enoxaparin) is usually preferred in pregnancy because it is given by subcutaneous injection and needs less monitoring. Warfarin (C) crosses the placenta and is teratogenic (warfarin embryopathy, particularly in weeks 6 to 12) and can cause fetal bleeding, so it is avoided (except in some women with mechanical heart valves, under specialist care). Protamine sulphate (B) is the antidote for heparin overdose, not an anticoagulant. Desirudin (D) is a direct thrombin inhibitor with insufficient safety data in pregnancy.

questions.text: Statins are administered at night because:

options.A: They cause sedation to promote sleep
options.B: Cortisol levels in blood inhibit its action
options.C: Hepatic cholesterol synthesis occurs at night
options.D: They cause exertional angina when taken during the day

questions.explanation: Hepatic cholesterol synthesis occurs at night (C) is correct because the liver makes most cholesterol during the night, when HMG-CoA reductase activity is at its highest, and statins work by competitively inhibiting this enzyme. Statins with a short half-life (simvastatin, lovastatin, fluvastatin) work best when taken in the evening, so that their blood level is highest when cholesterol production peaks; atorvastatin and rosuvastatin have long half-lives and can be taken at any time of day. They do not cause sedation (A). Cortisol (B) does not inhibit their action. They do not cause exertional angina (D). The nurse should teach the patient to report unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness (myopathy, rhabdomyolysis) and dark urine, to avoid grapefruit juice (with simvastatin and atorvastatin), and to have liver function checked.

questions.text: A true statement regarding Loperamide is:

options.A: Causes CNS effects such as depression
options.B: Continue the drug if diarrhea persists for more than 24 hours
options.C: It is indicated for diarrhea caused by antibiotic therapy
options.D: It is contra indicated among patients with hypertension

questions.explanation: Causes CNS effects such as depression (A) is the best answer. Loperamide is an opioid-receptor agonist in the gut wall that slows motility. It is largely kept out of the brain by the P-glycoprotein pump, so it normally has minimal CNS effects, but it can cause drowsiness and dizziness, and in overdose, in very young children and with drugs that block P-glycoprotein, it can cause CNS and respiratory depression, so it is avoided in children under 2 years and doses must not be exceeded. Continue the drug if diarrhea persists for more than 24 hours (B) is incorrect because if diarrhoea persists (generally beyond 48 hours), the patient should stop the drug and seek medical review, since continuing masks a possible infection or other cause. It is indicated for diarrhea caused by antibiotic therapy (C) is incorrect because loperamide can worsen pseudomembranous colitis (Clostridioides difficile), by trapping the toxin in the gut, and is contraindicated in dysentery and bloody diarrhoea. It is contra indicated among patients with hypertension (D) is incorrect; high blood pressure is not a contraindication. Oral rehydration remains the main treatment for diarrhoea.

questions.text: The main reason for rotating the injection site in insulin administration is to:
questions.explanation: Prevent lipodystrophy (B) is correct because repeated insulin injection into the same area causes changes in the subcutaneous fat: lipohypertrophy (fatty lumps) or lipoatrophy (loss of fat, dents). Insulin is poorly and unpredictably absorbed from these areas, which causes erratic blood glucose control. The patient should rotate sites within an area (abdomen, thighs, upper arms, buttocks), keep injections about 2 to 3 cm from the last site, check the skin regularly, and use a new needle each time. Prevent hypoglycemia (A) is incorrect, because rotation does not prevent low blood sugar (although absorption into scarred tissue can cause unpredictable levels). Prevent injury on one site (C) is a minor benefit, but not the main reason. Minimize lactic acidosis (D) is incorrect, since lactic acidosis is associated with metformin, not insulin injection sites.
